intro: Hong Kong's old trees are shaped by the same shortage of flat ground that shapes the rest of the city: banyans root straight into the mortar of century-old stone retaining walls, and New Territories villages keep camphor groves behind their houses as feng shui protection. The government's Old and Valuable Trees register tracks several hundred by district. These range from a wall of banyans an MTR station was rerouted to avoid, and a fig grown through an abandoned seventeenth-century stone house, to a rubber fig on the Peak whose roots have crossed Lugard Road.
meta_description: Hong Kong's most remarkable old trees, from a banyan wall an MTR station rerouted around to a fig tree engulfing an abandoned 17th-century house.
question_answer: Hong Kong's oldest documented tree is the King Banyan of Kowloon Park, an Indian laurel fig estimated at around 400 years old, growing above the spectator stand of the park's mini soccer pitch in Tsim Sha Tsui. The government recognised it as the city's largest urban tree by trunk girth in 1997.
question_meta: The King Banyan of Kowloon Park, an Indian laurel fig of about 400 years, is Hong Kong's oldest documented tree, named its largest urban tree in 1997.
question_context: A third of the King Banyan's trunk collapsed in a typhoon in 2007, and what survives is still recognised as Hong Kong's largest urban tree, a title the government gave it in 1997 after arborists put its age at around four hundred years. The tree grows above the spectator stand of a mini soccer pitch in Kowloon Park, on ground that was British military land, part of the former Whitfield Barracks, from the 1890s until 1967, three years before the Urban Council turned the site into the park itself. So the banyan is old enough to have shaded soldiers on parade long before it ever shaded families with strollers. It is currently infected with brown root rot, a fungal disease that has killed several of Hong Kong's other old trees, and sits under continuous government monitoring and treatment rather than removal, after conservation groups pushed for exactly that when the infection was first detected. Its crown still spans wide enough over the pitch to be unmistakable from the park's main path, cracked trunk, iron bracing and all, one of roughly 460 trees on Hong Kong's own public Old and Valuable Trees register.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Hong Kong?
faq.a: By documented estimate, the King Banyan of Kowloon Park, an Indian laurel fig the government recognised as the city's largest urban tree in 1997, at around 400 years old. Local tradition claims an even older age for a camphor tree in Sha Lo Wan on Lantau Island, over a thousand years, but that figure has no scientific dating behind it.

faq.q: Does Hong Kong have an official register of old trees?
faq.a: Yes. The Old and Valuable Trees register, run jointly by the Development Bureau and departments including the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, has tracked several hundred protected trees on government land since 2004, each individually mapped, inspected and re-surveyed.

faq.q: What are Hong Kong's stone wall trees?
faq.a: Banyans and figs that took root directly in the mortar of the city's many stone retaining walls, built into hillsides where flat ground was scarce. Roots eventually spread through the masonry itself; Forbes Street in Kennedy Town, with 27 trees on one wall, is the largest example.

faq.q: Are Hong Kong's old trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Every tree on this list can be reached without a ticket, on streets, in parks and gardens, on a trail and in village playgrounds. The pink shower tree at The Murray grows on hotel ground, so how close you get is the hotel's call. Sha Lo Wan, Lai Chi Wo and Mui Wo take a ferry or a hike.

trees.name: The King Banyan of Kowloon Park
trees.age_estimate: about 400 years (recognised as Hong Kong's largest urban tree in 1997)

location.address: Kowloon Park, above the spectator stand of the mini soccer pitch, Tsim Sha Tsui

trees.story: A third of this banyan's trunk came down in a 2007 typhoon, and what remains is still recognised as Hong Kong's largest urban tree by trunk girth, a title the government's own tree register gave it in 1997 when arborists put its age at around four hundred years. Indian laurel figs are common street trees across the city, planted by the thousand along roads and in parks, but almost none of them are left to grow old and wide the way this one has, standing above the spectator stand of Kowloon Park's mini soccer pitch since long before the park existed. The ground beneath it was British military land from the 1890s until 1967, part of the former Whitfield Barracks, three years before the Urban Council turned the site into a public park. The tree is old enough to have shaded soldiers on parade before it ever shaded families with strollers. It is now fighting a slower fight than the typhoon: brown root rot, a fungal disease that has spread through several of Hong Kong's oldest trees, has been detected in its roots, and the government has kept it under continuous monitoring and treatment rather than felling it, a decision conservation groups pushed hard for when the disease was first found. The crown still spreads wide enough over the pitch to be unmistakable, cracked trunk and all.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10 minute walk from MTR Tsim Sha Tsui station, via Haiphong Road entrance
trees.notes: Age (about 400 years) and 'largest urban tree' status from SCMP's 2015 report on the 1997 government recognition, corroborated by the Conservancy Association's own campaign page describing the tree's brown root rot treatment. Coordinates converted from the government's own Old and Valuable Trees register (OVTNo LCSD YTM/97, HK1980 Grid easting 835547 / northing 818183, data.gov.hk / greening.gov.hk, free reuse with attribution per data.gov.hk's terms and conditions) using a Transverse Mercator inverse transform implemented and sanity-checked this session (origin round-trip exact; several other converted points cross-checked against independently known Hong Kong locations). Whitfield Barracks dates (1890s construction, returned to government 1967, redeveloped into Kowloon Park 1970) corroborated via Wikipedia and Hong Kong Antiquities and Monuments Office material. Photo search this session found no clearly identifiable, individually-tagged open photo of this specific banyan among Kowloon Park's many trees; stays an honest gap.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its cracked, partly missing trunk, a third torn away by a 2007 typhoon, still the widest in the city. It stands above the spectator stand of Kowloon Park's mini soccer pitch.

trees.name: The Stone Wall Trees of Forbes Street
trees.age_estimate: wall dates to the 1890s; several trees individually over 100 years

location.address: Forbes Street, near Exit C of Kennedy Town MTR station, Kennedy Town

trees.story: When engineers first drew up plans to extend the MTR through Kennedy Town, a wall of nearly thirty banyan trees stood directly in the way, and after a 2005 flash-mob campaign by the Conservancy Association, the MTR rerouted the station underneath the old Kennedy Town Swimming Pool instead and built an exit specifically to leave the wall alone. Twenty-seven Chinese banyans and figs grow straight out of three stone masonry retaining walls along Forbes Street, roots fused into brickwork some records date to the 1890s, when the street was first laid out near the American Forbes family's Hong Kong Rope Works. It is the largest tree wall of its kind in the city, out of roughly 1,200 masonry wall trees recorded across Hong Kong, and several of its oldest specimens are individually listed on the government's own Old and Valuable Trees register. Stone wall trees grow the way this dense, hillside city forced them to. A seed lands in a crack, roots spread through mortar instead of soil, and given enough decades the tree and the wall become one structure, impossible to remove one without damaging the other. That, as much as the 2005 campaign, is what actually saved this one. It stands on an ordinary residential street a few minutes from the tram terminus, walls and trees together, exactly where the fight to keep them left them.
trees.access: Free, public street, viewable at any time
trees.transport: At Exit C of MTR Kennedy Town station (Island Line)
trees.notes: Ensemble entry (27 individual banyans/figs on one wall), the collectible point is the wall itself, matching the site's ensemble bar (Amsterdam's Lomanstraat, Barcelona's Ciutadella silk tree precedent) since it is compact, famous for being exactly that, with one obvious place to stand. MTR rerouting and 2005 campaign corroborated by the Conservancy Association's own project page (cahk.org.hk) and an independent local heritage site (stonewalltreehk.com). Several individual trees on this wall carry their own OVT/SWT register entries (e.g. Department Ref ARCHSD CW/44, CW/45, CW/47), confirming government recognition, though this entry treats the wall as one collectible ensemble rather than listing each tree separately. Coordinates are the register's own grid point for the OVT-listed tree nearest the playground entrance (ARCHSD CW/47), converted from HK1980 Grid as described in hkg_001's notes. Photo viewed directly 2026-07-31: the wall's cascading roots are unmistakably the subject, daylight, colour, well framed, passes the Cadiz standard.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by their trunks and roots fused directly into three stone masonry retaining walls. They stand along Forbes Street, near Exit C of Kennedy Town MTR station.

trees.name: The Kam Tin Tree House
trees.age_estimate: the banyan is over 100 years old; the stone ruin it engulfs is late Ming dynasty

location.address: Shui Mei Village Playground, Kam Tin, Yuen Long

trees.story: Nobody agrees on what this stone house was originally for, a temple, a study hall, a family residence, but everybody agrees on why it stands empty: in 1661, the new Qing dynasty ordered Hong Kong's coastline evacuated to cut off supplies reaching Ming loyalist rebels, and the Tang clan family who owned this house in Kam Tin left with everyone else. Villagers were kept from the coast for eight years, and by the time the order lifted, whoever had lived here never came back. The building sat abandoned long enough that, at some point in the following centuries, a Chinese banyan took root in it, and it has spent more than a hundred years since growing directly through the structure rather than around it, trunk and roots forcing themselves through gaps in the brickwork until tree and ruin became a single object. What is left today reads less like a house with a tree beside it than a tree that happens to have kept a house's walls as part of its own shape, roof long gone, window openings now just holes the trunk grows past. It stands in a public playground in Shui Mei Village, a short trip by minibus from Yuen Long or Kam Sheung Road, one of the more unusual things a seventeenth-century eviction order has ever produced.
trees.access: Free, public playground
trees.transport: By minibus from Yuen Long or Kam Sheung Road MTR station towards Kam Tin, short walk from Shui Mei Village
trees.notes: 1661 Qing coastal evacuation order and the tree's 100+ year age corroborated across two independent travel/history sources (Hong Kong Footprint, Chestnut Journal) plus the official Hong Kong Tourism-linked gohk.gov.hk district guide. Coordinates from the government's own Old and Valuable Trees register (OVTNo LCSD YL/6, 'Shui Mei Village Playground', HK1980 Grid 824313/834252), converted as described in hkg_001's notes; this is the same public playground the sources describe, so identity is not in question even though the register entry does not itself name the tree house. Photo viewed directly 2026-07-31: the roots and trunk consuming the ruin are unmistakably the subject, daylight, colour, well framed, passes the Cadiz standard.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk and roots growing straight through the walls and window openings of an abandoned stone ruin. It stands in Shui Mei Village Playground, Kam Tin.

trees.name: The Camphor of She Shan Tsuen
trees.age_estimate: estimated 300-500 years, most often cited as about 400

location.address: She Shan Fung Shui Woodland, She Shan Tsuen, Lam Tsuen, Tai Po

trees.story: Ten adults linking arms cannot fully encircle this camphor's trunk, and the tree they would be hugging predates every building in the village it half-hides. She Shan Tsuen's feng shui woodland, 5.7 hectares the government protected as a Site of Special Scientific Interest in 1975, exists because villages across Hong Kong's New Territories deliberately left a strip of hillside forest standing behind their houses, believing an intact wood at a settlement's back shielded it from bad fortune and worse weather. Camphor trees anchor most of these feng shui woods, chosen centuries ago for their size and longevity rather than planted at random, and She Shan's has grown into one of the largest examples in the New Territories: a 32 metre crown, seven storeys of glossy waxy leaves, and an age historical references put between three and five centuries, most often cited at around four hundred years. Government inspectors have logged a severe cavity and dead branches in recent surveys, the ordinary wear of a tree old enough that nobody alive remembers it being young, and it remains under continuous monitoring and pruning rather than removal. It stands on the wooded slope directly behind the village, a short walk off Lam Kam Road, still doing the job it was left standing there to do.
trees.access: Free, reachable via a footpath behind the village; part of a protected Site of Special Scientific Interest, please keep to the path
trees.transport: By minibus or car to Lam Tsuen off Lam Kam Road, then a short walk to She Shan village
trees.notes: Age (300-500 years, commonly cited as 400), crown size (32m) and trunk girth (ten adults linking arms) come from one detailed source, culture-hongkong.com; a second search pass through Wikipedia's She Shan Tsuen article and the government's own Herbarium fung shui woods overview confirmed the woodland's 1975 SSSI designation and the village's location but added no independent corroboration of the individual tree's age or size, so this stays flagged for a single-source age claim rather than presented as fully cross-verified. Existence, species and exact location are independently confirmed via the government's own Old and Valuable Trees register (OVTNo LANDSD TP/1, 'She Shan Tsuen, Tai Po, She Shan Fung Shui Woodland SSSI', condition notes matching: severe cavity, dead branches), coordinates converted from its HK1980 Grid reference (833000/834524) as described in hkg_001's notes. A future session should look for a second independent source on the specific age figure before upgrading this out of flagged.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, too wide for ten adults linking arms to encircle, under a 32 metre crown. It stands behind She Shan Tsuen village, off Lam Kam Road.

trees.name: The King Camphor of Sha Lo Wan
trees.age_estimate: undated; local and official tourism material claims over 1,000 years but no scientific dating exists

location.address: The slope next to Sha Lo Wan School, Sha Lo Wan, Lantau Island

trees.story: Japanese soldiers cut down most of Lantau Island's large trees for fuel during the wartime occupation, and by local account, they stopped short of this one because they believed a guardian spirit haunted it and would frighten off anyone who tried. Whether the spirit or something more practical spared it, the camphor beside Sha Lo Wan's old village school survived a period when little large timber on the island did, and villagers still call it Sha Lo Wan's King Camphor. Hong Kong's own tourism authority repeats the village's claim that it is over a thousand years old, a figure with no scientific dating behind it and best treated as local tradition rather than a measured fact, though camphors are long-lived enough that a large old specimen reaching many centuries is far from implausible. What is certain is its role: Sha Lo Wan, a fishing village on Lantau's quiet north-west coast reachable by a coastal footpath or a rural kaido ferry from Tung Chung, has treated this tree as a feng shui guardian for generations, the kind of tree a village builds its sense of protection around rather than fells for a hard winter. It still stands on the government-registered slope beside the school, watched over rather than the other way around now.
trees.access: Free, public village land
trees.transport: By kaido ferry from Tung Chung to Sha Lo Wan, or via the Lantau coastal footpath
trees.notes: The '1,000+ years' figure is a local/official claim, sourced to the government's own South Development and Sustainable Lantau Office (CEDD) storytelling page, repeated by other tourism material, but not a scientifically dated figure; the story presents it explicitly as a claim rather than a fact per the honesty rule. age_min/age_max are deliberately kept to a conservative, defensible 200-300 rather than encoding the unverified 1,000-year figure into age_max: this field feeds mechanical site-wide comparisons (the per-city oldest-tree page, any future oldest-trees-in-the-world collection), and hard rule 8 requires superlative-driving numbers to be checked rather than passed through from an unverified local claim. hong-kong.json sets oldest_tree_id to hkg_001 for the same reason, so this entry's own claimed age never silently drives the city's 'oldest tree' answer. The WWII guardian-spirit story is independently corroborated by a second, unrelated source (a personal blog, nstecker.com, predating and unconnected to the government page). Existence, species and exact location confirmed via the government's own Old and Valuable Trees register (OVTNo AFCD/KS/005, 'The slope next to Sha Lo Wan School, Lantau Island', condition notes: minor cavity, fair health, sign of termite infestation), coordinates converted from its HK1980 Grid reference (808051/816127) as described in hkg_001's notes.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing on the slope directly beside Sha Lo Wan's old village school. It stands in Sha Lo Wan, on Lantau Island's north-west coast.

trees.name: The Five-Finger Camphor of Lai Chi Wo
trees.age_estimate: undocumented; a mature specimen already large enough to be targeted during the WWII occupation

location.address: Lai Chi Wo village feng shui woodland, Sha Tau Kok, North District
location.neighbourhood: Lai Chi Wo, Sha Tau Kok

trees.story: Only one of this camphor's original five trunks is missing, and the reason it lost that one and not the rest is the whole story: during the Japanese occupation, soldiers came to cut the tree for fuel, and Lai Chi Wo's villagers physically stood between them and the trunk. They lost the argument over a single branch. Four still remain, splayed from a shared base wide enough that the tree is simply known as the Five-Finger Camphor, and it has stood in the feng shui woodland behind this Hakka village since before anyone alive can date it. Hakka settlers built Lai Chi Wo in the 16th century, grew it to more than two hundred houses and over a thousand residents by laying the village out on strict geomantic lines, and then watched it empty through the 1960s and 70s as families left for the city and abroad. The camphor stayed, along with the rest of the feng shui wood's more than a hundred native plant species, and it has become the emblem of a rural revival effort that has slowly repopulated and restored the village since the 2010s. Reaching it means a ferry from Ma Liu Shui or a hike in from Wu Kau Tang, through one of the last intact Hakka settlements left in Hong Kong's New Territories, to stand under four fingers where there used to be five.
trees.access: Free, within an active countryside conservation and rural revival area
trees.transport: By ferry from Ma Liu Shui (weekends and public holidays) or a hike from Wu Kau Tang
trees.notes: WWII branch-loss story and village history corroborated across two independent sources (EJ Insight news article, 360Cities panorama caption); village settlement date and rural-revival programme also appear on Hong Kong Tourism Board's own Lai Chi Wo page. No source gives a specific planting date or age for the tree itself, so age_min/age_max left at 0 rather than guessed, per the honesty rule (same convention as Singapore's undated heritage-register entries). Existence, species and exact location confirmed via the government's own Old and Valuable Trees register (OVTNo AFCD/LK/009, TR no. AFCD/N/00002, 'Lai Chi Wo, Sha Tau Kok', condition notes: asymmetric canopy, minor cavity, moderate decay), coordinates converted from its HK1980 Grid reference (844630/842966) as described in hkg_001's notes.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its four trunks splaying from one shared base, a fifth cut away during the wartime occupation. It stands behind Lai Chi Wo village, Sha Tau Kok.

trees.name: The Stonewall Fig of Ka Wai Man Road

location.address: Ka Wai Man Road Garden, Kennedy Town

trees.story: Hong Kong's government files this tree under two categories at once, and the second is the interesting half. The Old and Valuable Trees register lists it as OVT and SWT together, Old and Valuable Tree and Stonewall Tree, and the department responsible for it is not the one that runs the city's parks. It is the Architectural Services Department, which looks after government masonry. The whole story sits in that administrative detail: this fig is maintained by the people who maintain walls, because a wall is what it grows out of. The measurements are serious. A trunk 1.8 metres through, seventeen metres tall, a crown spreading twenty-four metres, and an inspection record noting three separate leans, one growing toward the light, one a response to load, and one the tree corrected by itself, which is what decades of pushing out of vertical stonework and rebalancing looks like written down. No age has ever been published for it. It sits above Ka Wai Man Road in Kennedy Town, a hundred metres from the Forbes Street wall, so it extends that walk rather than repeating it. One caveat to carry along. This corner of Kennedy Town has been an active redevelopment site since late 2022, and although the register inspected the tree in March 2023, after the work started, check the garden is open before making the trip for this tree alone.

trees.transport: Short walk from MTR Kennedy Town station Exit C, one street over from the Forbes Street stone wall trees

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a fig growing out of a stone retaining wall, maintained by the department that looks after masonry rather than parks. It stands in the Ka Wai Man Road Garden, Kennedy Town.

trees.name: The Banyan of King George V Park

location.address: King George V Memorial Park, Canton Road, Jordan, Kowloon

trees.story: This park opened in June 1941 and was a rubbish dump by Christmas. King George V Memorial Park in Jordan was finished late, its opening on 11 June delayed because the governor was ill, and six months later Hong Kong fell to the Japanese and the new park was put to other use for the duration. The Urban Council rebuilt it after the war, added three Chinese-styled kiosks and reopened it on 21 March 1954, then extended it westward in the 1970s when Canton Road was realigned, and redesigned it again in the 1990s after the airport programme reclaimed the land beyond it. Through four versions of the park, this fig has stayed put. The government's tree register gives it a trunk 1.8 metres through, thirteen metres tall, an eighteen metre crown and normal vigour at its last inspection in November 2022. It gives no age, and no other source names the tree individually, so its years are undocumented. One thing to get right before setting off: Hong Kong has two parks named after King George V. This is the Kowloon one, on Canton Road in Jordan, a couple of minutes further on from the King Banyan of Kowloon Park. The other is across the harbour in Sai Ying Pun, with its own trees and its own history.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Short walk from MTR Jordan station, or from the northern end of Kowloon Park via Canton Road
trees.verify_notes: Height 13.0 m from the hongkong-ovt register, matched on our own pin (0 m away). 2026-10-20: LCSD YTM/98 was not among the 959 trees on the register's detail pages (ovt.greening.gov.hk detail ids 1 to 1199 scanned; data/research/hong-kong-ovt-status.json), so its Alive status is unconfirmed this year. Absence from the site is not a removal; check before any retirement.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, 1.8 metres through, under an 18 metre crown, in the Kowloon version of the park rather than the one in Sai Ying Pun. It stands on Canton Road, Jordan.

trees.name: The Camphor of Kowloon Park Drive

location.address: Kowloon Park Drive Children's Playground, Kowloon Park, Tsim Sha Tsui

trees.story: The three camphors already on this page stand behind villages, kept for centuries as feng shui trees. This one stands beside a children's playground, and it is thicker than any of them. Two metres of trunk diameter, sixteen metres tall, a twenty metre crown and normal vigour at its last inspection in October 2022, at the southern end of Kowloon Park near the aviary, which puts it a ten minute walk from the King Banyan at the far end of the same park. Camphor was an industrial commodity long before it was a park tree. The wood and leaves are distilled for camphor itself, and before synthetics took over, that substance was the essential plasticiser for celluloid, which meant photographic film, and a stabiliser for smokeless powder, which meant ammunition. The two together made camphor a strategic material worth controlling, most of the world's supply came out of Taiwan and Japan under state monopoly, and the trees were felled to get it. So a large old camphor is not a neutral object in this part of the world. It is a tree that was worth more cut down than standing and did not get cut. No age is recorded for this one, and a second, smaller camphor stands in the same playground. Crush a fallen leaf and the smell settles the identification instantly.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: 10-15 min walk from MTR Tsim Sha Tsui station, within Kowloon Park via Kowloon Park Drive, at the southern end of the park from the King Banyan

trees.name: The Banyan of Nathan Road

location.address: Park Lane Shopper's Boulevard, Nathan Road, opposite St Andrew's Church, Tsim Sha Tsui

trees.story: The government's inspection of this tree reads like a description of the street it is on. Compacted soil. Cable and brace support fitted. More than seventy-five percent of the ground under its crown built over or paved. Overall risk moderate, vigour normal, which together describe a large healthy tree living in conditions no tree would choose. It stands on the Park Lane Shopper's Boulevard stretch of Nathan Road, the Golden Mile, with a trunk 2.07 metres through, nineteen metres tall and a crown spreading twenty-two metres over one of Hong Kong's busiest shopping streets. Directly opposite is St Andrew's Church, built between 1904 and 1906 in Victorian Gothic on a small rise above the road, Kowloon's oldest Anglican church and a gift to the community from Paul Chater, the Armenian-born businessman who co-founded Hong Kong Land and paid for a good deal of what the colony became. So the view is a banyan against English stonework, on a street that now sells watches and phones. The register gives no age for the tree, and no independent source names it, so what is documented is its size and its condition. It is a six or seven minute walk from the King Banyan in Kowloon Park, which makes it the easy last stop of that walk rather than a trip of its own.
trees.access: Free, public street, viewable at any time
trees.transport: A few minutes' walk from MTR Tsim Sha Tsui station Exit A1, on Nathan Road's Park Lane Shopper's Boulevard stretch
trees.verify_notes: Height 19.0 m from the hongkong-ovt register, matched on our own pin (0 m away).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crown, spreading 22 metres over one of Hong Kong's busiest streets, cabled and braced for support. It stands on the Park Lane Shopper's Boulevard, Nathan Road, opposite St Andrew's Church.

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Development Bureau, Greening, Landscape and Tree Management Section), no. LCSD YTM/6 (Tree Register No. LCSD/YTM/00061)

trees.name: The Rubber Fig of Lugard Road

location.address: Lugard Road (Hong Kong Trail) near No. 28, Victoria Peak

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. LCSD CW/134

trees.access: Free. Lugard Road is a public footpath (part of Hong Kong Trail section 1), open at all hours; the tree grows across the path.
trees.transport: About 1 km straight-line west of the Peak Tower and Peak Tram upper terminus along Lugard Road (a level walk); Peak Tram from Garden Road, Central.
trees.story:
No tree in Hong Kong's register of old and valuable trees has a wider trunk than this one, and strictly speaking it does not have one trunk at all. The register measures five metres across at chest height. What it is measuring is a crowd: aerial roots that dropped from the branches, reached the ground and thickened into trunks of their own, until the tree had grown clean across Lugard Road. The Urban Trees of the World blog described the result in 2017 as a tunnel over the road.

Compare the species' ordinary numbers. The government's own plant page gives a typical India-rubber tree a main trunk 25 to 40 centimetres through. This one stands 25 metres tall under a crown 28 metres wide, and the register lists it for two reasons, large size and outstanding form, neither of which needs explaining once you are standing in it.

India-rubber trees come from north-east India and South-east Asia. Their white latex was once tapped for gum on plantations around the world, until the poor quality of the rubber ended the trade. The tree became a street tree instead, because drought, shade and polluted air barely bother it. A few other big rubber trees share this hillside, but this is the one the path runs through.

Lugard Road is a level footpath on the Hong Kong Trail, about a kilometre from the Peak Tram. Nobody has put a date on the tree; if you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunks, aerial roots grown into a mass five metres across that spans the footpath. It stands on Lugard Road, about a kilometre west of the Peak Tower.

trees.name: The Big-leaved Banyan of Hong Kong Park's Tai Chi Garden

location.address: Hong Kong Park, outside the perimeter wall of the Tai Chi Garden, 19 Cotton Tree Drive, Central

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. LCSD CW/103

trees.access: Free. Hong Kong Park outdoor areas are open 6:00 to 23:00 daily (travel-site listings, official LCSD page not readable this pass); the tree stands outside the Tai Chi Garden wall.
trees.transport: MTR Admiralty, Exit C1, then through Pacific Place and up the escalators to the park (about 10 minutes).
trees.story:
This fig is twenty metres tall and thirty-four metres wide, a crown that has spent its life going sideways rather than up. Underneath it is a trunk 2.71 metres across at chest height, which makes it the thickest tree on the government's old and valuable register anywhere in Central and Western district, bar one: the rubber tree that has grown across Lugard Road on the Peak.

It is also a local. The big-leaved fig is native to Hong Kong, unlike the India-rubber tree, and among the local banyans it is the one that drops its leaves.

It stands outside the perimeter wall of Hong Kong Park's Tai Chi Garden, and it has company. Within about 140 metres the register counts four more banyans, a second big-leaved fig 22 metres tall, a kapok, and three trees growing out of stone walls a few metres from this one. The tallest of those banyans, 70 metres away, has its own entry on this page, and so does the kapok. None of them comes close to this trunk.

The park's outdoor areas open from six in the morning until eleven at night, and the tree was inspected and recorded alive in May 2026. Nobody has recorded its age; if you know it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crown, 34 metres wide over a trunk 2.71 metres through, the thickest registered trunk in the park. It stands just outside the wall of Hong Kong Park's Tai Chi Garden.

trees.name: The Tall Banyan of Hong Kong Park

location.address: Hong Kong Park, 19 Cotton Tree Drive, Central

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. ARCHSD CW/39

trees.access: Free. Hong Kong Park outdoor areas open 6:00 to 23:00 daily (travel-site listings).
trees.transport: MTR Admiralty, Exit C1, through Pacific Place and up the escalators (about 10 minutes).
trees.story:
Seventy metres from the thickest fig in Hong Kong Park stands a banyan with a much thinner trunk that beats it on everything else. This one is 28 metres tall, the tallest of the park's registered banyans, and its crown spreads 35 metres, the widest of them too. Its trunk is 1.78 metres across at chest height, about a metre less than its neighbour's. Height and spread, it turns out, do not follow girth.

It is an Indian laurel fig, the same species as the King Banyan across the harbour in Kowloon Park. Even its paperwork differs from its neighbour: the register names the Architectural Services Department as its keeper, while the big-leaved fig beside it belongs to the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, which runs the park.

The pair make a short stop of their own. Stand under the big-leaved fig outside the Tai Chi Garden wall, look for the taller crown 70 metres off, and you have seen two of the biggest registered trees in Central for the price of one detour. A kapok and three more registered banyans grow within the same corner of the park.

The tree was inspected and recorded alive at the end of August 2026. Nobody has put an age on it; if you can, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height: at 28 metres it is the tallest of Hong Kong Park's registered banyans, with the widest crown, 35 metres. It stands about 70 metres from the big-leaved fig by the Tai Chi Garden.

trees.name: The Kapok Tree of Hong Kong Park

location.address: Hong Kong Park, 19 Cotton Tree Drive, Central

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. ARCHSD CW/36

trees.access: Free. Hong Kong Park outdoor areas open 6:00 to 23:00 daily (travel-site listings).
trees.transport: MTR Admiralty, Exit C1, through Pacific Place and up the escalators (about 10 minutes).
trees.story:
The road that runs past Hong Kong Park, Cotton Tree Drive, takes its name from this kind of tree. Kapok is the cotton tree, and this one stands 23 metres tall inside the park. Nothing on record ties this particular kapok to the road's name, but it shows you what the name means.

Among the park's registered trees it is the odd one out. The banyans and figs around it are built for width, with trunks up to 2.71 metres across and crowns spreading more than thirty metres. The kapok has a trunk 86 centimetres through and a crown only 15 metres wide. It has put almost everything into height. Another registered kapok in the park reaches 16 metres on a thinner trunk, so this is the taller of the two by seven metres.

Kapoks flower on bare branches in late winter, after the leaves have dropped, so in flower the tree looks nothing like the banyans beside it. Nobody has fixed when this one flowers. If you have stood under it in bloom, tell us the month.

The park's outdoor areas open from six in the morning until eleven at night, and the tree was inspected and recorded alive at the end of August 2026. The register gives no age, and the month of its flowers is the question we would most like answered.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its slim trunk, 86 centimetres through, rising 23 metres among much wider banyans and figs. It stands in Hong Kong Park, the taller of the park's two registered kapoks.

trees.name: The Pink Shower Tree of The Murray
trees.species: Pink Shower Tree (Cassia javanica var. indochinensis)

location.address: Forecourt outside the lobby of The Murray (former Murray Building), 22 Cotton Tree Drive, Central

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Development Bureau), LANDSD(LEASED) CW/1, Tree Register No. LANDSD/CW/00004

trees.access: Free to look at from the open area outside the hotel lobby (a Development Bureau blog describes the tree as standing in the open area outside the lobby). The ground is the hotel's (Lands Department lease); whether the forecourt is open to non-guests at all hours was not confirmed.
trees.transport: Beside the Peak Tram lower terminus on Garden Road; about 10 minutes' walk from MTR Admiralty or Central (estimate, not timed by a source).
trees.story:
This tree spent decades standing on its own in a government car park, and it now grows up through two levels of a hotel. The building beside it went up in 1969 as Murray Building, a block of government offices on Cotton Tree Drive where several policy bureaux had their headquarters. The tree was already there. Hong Kong's Secretary for Development, who once had an office in the building, wrote after its conversion that the tree is over a hundred years old and saw the building completed. That is the only age anyone has given it, so read it as an account rather than a measurement.

It is a pink and white shower tree, Cassia javanica var. indochinensis, 17 metres tall with a trunk just over a metre across at chest height. Its health, the Secretary wrote, had only been so-so. When the offices became The Murray hotel, which opened in January 2018 after four years of work, the developer took special care around it, and the car park became a forecourt with a podium above, so the tree now passes through both levels. By that account it came out of the works in leaf and flower, and it was flowering again in May 2022.

The tree stands in the open area outside the hotel lobby, on the hotel's own ground. How close you can get, and at what hours, is the hotel's call. The Peak Tram's lower terminus on Garden Road is next door.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk rising through two levels, the hotel forecourt and the podium above it. It stands in the open area outside the lobby of The Murray, 22 Cotton Tree Drive.
trees.pin_source: Register coordinate for LANDSD(LEASED) CW/1; an HKU Digital Arboretum video at the tree (2022) is placed 6 m from it.

trees.name: The Roadside Banyan of Garden Road

location.address: Garden Road, next to St. John's Building, Central

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. LCSD CW/79

trees.access: Free. Roadside tree on a public road (Garden Road), visible from the pavement at all hours.
trees.transport: Garden Road is a 10 to 15 minute walk from MTR Central or Admiralty (estimate); Peak Tram lower terminus is about 150 m away.
trees.story:
The biggest banyan on this stretch of Garden Road is no longer here. The government's register of old and valuable trees still carries its entry, a trunk 2.1 metres across, with one word against it: removed. A second registered banyan on the road is marked the same way. This is the one still standing beside St. John's Building, and that alone is worth a moment on the pavement.

It is an Indian laurel fig, 22 metres tall, with a trunk 1.56 metres across at chest height and a crown spreading 24 metres. Garden Road runs past the Peak Tram's lower terminus, about 150 metres from this tree, and the banyans along it are roadside trees in the full sense: no park around them, just kerb, traffic and the buildings on either side. Two more registered banyans, slightly smaller, stand about 90 metres north-east, at the junction with Lower Albert Road, both recorded alive in 2026.

The Leisure and Cultural Services Department looks after it, and its last inspection, in September 2026, found it alive. The Murray's pink shower tree and the registered banyans of Hong Kong Park are all within about 270 metres.

Nobody has recorded this banyan's age. If you know it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, 1.56 metres through, on the pavement beside St. John's Building. The two smaller registered banyans are about 90 metres north-east, at the Lower Albert Road junction.

trees.name: The Sausage Tree of City Hall Memorial Garden

location.address: City Hall Memorial Garden, Edinburgh Place, Central

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Development Bureau), LCSD CW/124, Tree Register No. LCSD/CW/00093

trees.access: Free. A public garden beside Hong Kong City Hall run by LCSD (garden hours not checked this pass).
trees.transport: About 5 minutes' walk from MTR Central (Exit A) or Hong Kong station (estimate); Star Ferry Central pier is next to Edinburgh Place.
trees.story:
This tree is on Hong Kong's register of old and valuable trees without being big. It is 14 metres tall, with a trunk 85 centimetres across, a fraction of the banyans in Hong Kong Park. What it has instead is rarity. It is a sausage tree, a species the register seldom holds, growing in the garden beside City Hall a few steps from the Star Ferry pier.

The name is the description. Its flowers hang below the branches on long stalks, like lamps on cords, and the fruit that follows is long enough to explain the English name without help. Those dangling stalks are the quickest way to pick it out among the other trees in the garden. Its crown is 16 metres wide, wider than the tree is tall.

The City Hall Memorial Garden is on Edinburgh Place in Central, a public garden run by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, and the Star Ferry's Central pier is next to the square. The tree was inspected and recorded alive in July 2026.

Nobody has put an age on it, or recorded when a sausage tree was planted beside City Hall. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flowers and long fruit hanging below its branches on long stalks. It stands in the City Hall Memorial Garden on Edinburgh Place, the only sausage tree on the register there.
trees.pin_source: Register coordinate for LCSD CW/124; a geotagged Commons photograph of the tree (2020-10-23) stands 6 m from it, and an HKU Digital Arboretum video (2022) about 10 m.

trees.name: The Camphor of the Zoological and Botanical Gardens

location.address: Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens, near the octagonal pavilion, Albany Road, Central

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. LCSD CW/68

trees.access: Free. LCSD public garden (opening hours not checked this pass; the aviary and greenhouses may keep shorter hours than the grounds).
trees.transport: About 15 minutes' walk uphill from MTR Central along Garden Road / Upper Albert Road (estimate); several buses stop on Albany Road.
trees.story:
This camphor is held up by hardware. The government's register of old and valuable trees records braces and cables holding it, which tells you that somebody looked at an old tree needing help and decided it was worth the trouble. Under that support is a trunk 1.46 metres across at chest height, in a tree 18 metres tall with a crown 16 metres wide, beside the octagonal pavilion of the Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens.

The gardens hold several registered trees, and the register is frank about how that goes over time. Two of them, one a Parkia, now carry the word removed against their entries. The camphor was inspected in July 2026 and is recorded alive.

The other camphors on this page live very different lives. Three stand in villages in the New Territories and on Lantau, and one, thicker than this, grows beside a playground in Kowloon Park. This is the one in a formal garden, on Albany Road above Central, within walking distance of the offices below.

The gardens are free to enter; the aviary and greenhouses may keep shorter hours than the grounds. Nobody has recorded when this tree was planted. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the braces and cables that support it, on a trunk 1.46 metres through. It stands near the octagonal pavilion in the Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens.

trees.name: The Rubber Fig of Castle Peak Road, Kwai Chung

location.address: Castle Peak Road Sitting-out Area, Kwai Chung

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. LCSD KWT/3

trees.access: Free. A public LCSD sitting-out area beside Castle Peak Road (Kwai Chung section).
trees.transport: About 1 km straight-line from Kwai Hing MTR station (Tsuen Wan line); walking route and time not verified, the sitting-out area is uphill on the Castle Peak Road side.
trees.story:
The tallest India-rubber tree on Hong Kong's register of old and valuable trees does not stand on the Peak or in a famous park. It grows in a roadside sitting-out area on Castle Peak Road in Kwai Chung, 32 metres tall, with a crown spreading 43 metres.

Its trunk measures 4.85 metres across at chest height. That is 15 centimetres short of the rubber tree on Lugard Road, the widest in the whole register, and like that tree it is not one trunk so much as a crowd of them, a mass of stems built from aerial roots. Put the two side by side on paper and the Kwai Chung tree wins on everything but those 15 centimetres. It is seven metres taller than the Lugard Road tree, and its crown is fifteen metres wider.

The Lugard Road tree has a footpath running through it and a place on the Hong Kong Trail. This one has a sitting-out area run by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department and the traffic of Castle Peak Road. On height and spread, it is the bigger tree.

The sitting-out area is public and free. Kwai Hing MTR station is about a kilometre away as the crow flies, and the garden is uphill on the Castle Peak Road side. The tree was recorded alive at its August 2026 inspection. Nobody has dated it; if you can, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size: 32 metres tall, a crown 43 metres wide and a trunk mass of aerial roots 4.85 metres across. It stands in the Castle Peak Road Sitting-out Area, Kwai Chung.

trees.name: The Banyan of Mui Wo

location.address: Chung Hau Street, Mui Wo, Lantau Island

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. LCSD IS/2

trees.access: Free. Street tree on Chung Hau Street in Mui Wo village.
trees.transport: Ferry from Central Pier 6 to Mui Wo (ferry duration not verified this pass), then a short walk into Chung Hau.
trees.story:
Getting to this banyan means leaving Hong Kong Island by boat. It stands on Chung Hau Street in Mui Wo, a village on Lantau Island reached by ferry from Central's Pier 6, and its crown is wider than the tree is tall: 22 metres high, 28 metres across, over a street rather than a park lawn.

The government's register of old and valuable trees files it under the Islands district, and gives it a trunk 1.43 metres across at chest height. It is an Indian laurel fig, the same species as the King Banyan in Kowloon Park and the roadside banyans of Garden Road. The difference is the setting. Those trees share their ground with other registered giants; this one has a village street to itself, and the nearest other tree on the register is some 350 metres away.

The Leisure and Cultural Services Department looks after it as a street tree, and its last inspection, in April 2026, recorded it alive. It costs nothing to see: walk off the ferry into Mui Wo and find Chung Hau Street.

Nobody has written down how old it is. If you know its age, or what the street was like when it was young, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crown, 28 metres across and wider than the tree is tall, over Chung Hau Street. It stands in Mui Wo village, the only registered old tree within about 350 metres.
trees.pin_source: Register coordinate for LCSD IS/2; an iNaturalist observation of the tree (2022-11-29, GPS accuracy 3 m) stands 17 m from it, and HKU Digital Arboretum videos (2020, 2021) within 10 m.

trees.name: The Banyan of Signal Hill Garden

location.address: Signal Hill Garden, on a slope near the access road off Minden Row, Tsim Sha Tsui

official_register.name: Register of Old and Valuable Trees (Hong Kong Government), no. LCSD YTM/40

trees.access: Free. Signal Hill Garden is an LCSD public garden; the tree is on a slope beside the access road, exact reach from the paths not verified.
trees.transport: About 10 minutes' walk from MTR Tsim Sha Tsui (estimate; the garden is above Salisbury Road / Minden Row).
trees.story:
This banyan grows on a 40 metre hill that used to be a cape. Before land reclamation pushed Tsim Sha Tsui out into the harbour, Blackhead Point was the shoreline, and on top of it stands the Signal Hill Tower of 1907. From 1908 to 1933 a time ball dropped from its mast once or twice a day so ships' officers could check their chronometers; in the Second World War the tower stored ammunition, and in 2015 it was declared a monument.

The tree is on the slope below, beside the garden's access road off Minden Row. It is an Indian laurel fig, 18 metres tall, with a crown 21 metres wide and a trunk 1.95 metres across at chest height. That trunk is thicker than the Garden Road banyan across the harbour and thicker than the tallest banyan in Hong Kong Park, though this tree is shorter than either.

Because it grows on a slope by the access road rather than beside a lawn, you may see it better from the road than from under the crown, and how close the paths bring you is something to judge on the day. Signal Hill Garden is public and free, run by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, and the tree was inspected in July 2026 and recorded alive. The King Banyan in Kowloon Park is about a kilometre away.

Nobody has dated this tree. If you know its age, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, 1.95 metres through, on the slope beside the access road off Minden Row. It stands below the Signal Hill Tower, the red-brick time-ball tower at the top of the garden.
